q-143834.name: Question 1
q-143834.problem:
Find $\text{E}[XY],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3xy},\, & 1\le x\le y,\,e\le y\le {e}^{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
q-143834.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=xy.
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le y,\,e\le y\le {e}^{2}\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14161553/assets/09bf58b8505f860709d705f128b2bafbd6916382de56ba66d26a1a56319f0141.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}{\int }_{1}^{y}xy\cdot \frac{2}{3xy}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}{\int }_{1}^{y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}[x]_{x=1}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}(y-1)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]}_{y=e}^{y={e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{{e}^{4}}{2}-{e}^{2})-(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-e)] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{e}^{4}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{2}+e) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4}}{3}-{e}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}e.\end{aligned}
$$

q-143861.name: Question 2
q-143861.problem:
The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given in the table below. Find $\text{E}[X{e}^{Y}].$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.5$ | $0.1$ |
q-143861.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with supports ${S}_{X}$ and ${S}_{Y},$ respectively, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability mass function with support $S={S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}.$ If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}r(x,y)\,f(x,y).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X{e}^{Y}] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}r(x,y)\,f(x,y) \\  & =(1\cdot {e}^{0})\cdot f(1,0)+(1\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\cdot f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡3)+(2\cdot {e}^{0})\cdot f(2,0)+(2\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\cdot f(2,\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =1\cdot f(1,0)+3\cdot f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡3)+2\cdot f(2,0)+6\cdot f(2,\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =1\cdot 0.3+3\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.5+6\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0.3+0.3+1+0.6 \\  & =2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Suppose X and Y are discrete random variables with supports SX and SY, respectively, and f(x,y) is their joint probability mass function with support S=SX×SY. If r:R2→R is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

E[r(X,Y)]=∑(x,y)∈Sr(x,y)f(x,y).

In our case, we have

r(x,y)=xey.

Therefore, we obtain

E[XeY]=∑(x,y)∈Sr(x,y)f(x,y)=(1⋅e0)⋅f(1,0)+(1⋅eln⁡3)⋅f(1,ln⁡3)+(2⋅e0)⋅f(2,0)+(2⋅eln⁡3)⋅f(2,ln⁡3)=1⋅f(1,0)+3⋅f(1,ln⁡3)+2⋅f(2,0)+6⋅f(2,ln⁡3)=1⋅0.3+3⋅0.1+2⋅0.5+6⋅0.1=0.3+0.3+1+0.6=2.2.

q-143870.name: Question 3
q-143870.problem:
Find $\text{E}[X{Y}^{3}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9{y}^{2}},\, & 0\le x\le {y}^{3},\,0\le y\le 3; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
q-143870.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=x{y}^{3}.
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le {y}^{3},\,0\le y\le 3\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14161553/assets/68da52d856f882614241d72cff4dc3f5947cf16a6c9f58b0aea1c58d7eb375cc.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X{Y}^{3}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}x{y}^{3}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}x{y}^{3}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}}x{y}^{3}\cdot \frac{2}{9{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}y{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}y{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x={y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{7}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{[\frac{{y}^{8}}{8}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(\frac{{3}^{8}}{8}) \\  & =\frac{729}{8}.\end{aligned}

q-143874.name: Question 4
q-143874.problem:
Find $\text{E}[\frac{1}{XY}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}{y}^{3},\, & 0<x<1,\,0<y<2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
q-143874.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=\frac{1}{xy}.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\frac{1}{XY}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}\frac{1}{xy}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{xy}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{xy}\cdot \frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{4}{y}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{4}{y}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{8}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{3}}{8}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-143891.name: Question 5
q-143891.problem:
Find $\text{E}[X+3{Y}^{2}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{15},\, & 0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{x}{3}\le y\le 3; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
q-143891.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=x+3{y}^{2}.
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{x}{3}\le y\le 3\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14161553/assets/bc454de7a5ef0a9b0e2620bb44a0d0b481638ca04905bf6d986a52715a95c3db.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X+3{Y}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}(x+3{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{x/3}^{3}(x+3{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{2}{15}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{\int }_{0}^{3}[xy+{y}^{3}]_{y=x/3}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{\int }_{0}^{3}[3x+27-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{27}]\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+27x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{108}]}_{x=0}^{x=3} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}[\frac{27}{2}+81-3-\frac{3}{4}] \\  & =\frac{363}{30} \\  & =\frac{121}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$
